question: A 28-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 120 cells/µL) presents with progressive dyspnoea, dry cough and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest radiograph. BAL GMS stain reveals helmet-shaped cysts. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Helmet-shaped cysts on GMS stain in an HIV patient with CD4 <200 is diagnostic of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). High-dose TMP-SMX is the first-line treatment. Adjunctive corticosteroids (prednisolone) are added when PaO₂ is below 70 mmHg to reduce inflammation-mediated respiratory failure.

Amphotericin B is used for invasive fungal infections such as cryptococcosis, mucormycosis and invasive aspergillosis. It is not effective against Pneumocystis jirovecii, which requires folate pathway inhibition by TMP-SMX.
Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor used to treat influenza virus infection. The GMS stain showing helmet-shaped cysts confirms a fungal (Pneumocystis) aetiology, not a viral cause.
This four-drug regimen treats tuberculosis. The GMS stain findings (helmet-shaped cysts, not acid-fast bacilli) and the bilateral interstitial pattern point to PCP, not pulmonary TB.

overallFeedback.feedback: GMS stain showing helmet-shaped cysts in BAL of an immunocompromised patient is diagnostic of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. First-line treatment is high-dose co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) with adjunctive corticosteroids for hypoxaemic patients.

PCP is treated with high-dose TMP-SMX. GMS (Grocott's methenamine silver) stain is the diagnostic stain of choice, showing characteristic helmet-shaped or cup-shaped cysts. Prophylaxis with low-dose TMP-SMX should be initiated when CD4 falls below 200 cells/µL.
